content: Gestational weight gain is directly associated with fetal growth. Observational studies have shown that food supplementation during pregnancy can lead to increased gestational weight gain and improved fetal growth outcomes. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of dietary education to increase energy and protein intake, as well as the effects of actual energy and protein supplementation, on maternal and infant health outcomes. The review included 17 randomized controlled trials involving 9,030 women. The methodological quality of the included trials was assessed using Cochrane criteria and the GRADE approach. The overall risk of bias was unclear, and the quality of evidence for many outcomes was low. Nutritional Education Nutritional education during pregnancy was associated with a reduced risk of preterm birth (relative risk [RR] 0.46, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.21 to 0.98, low-quality evidence) and low birthweight (RR 0.04, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.14, low-quality evidence). One trial reported an increase in head circumference at birth (mean difference [MD] 0.99 cm, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.55). Birthweight significantly increased among undernourished women (MD 489.76 g, 95% CI 427.93 to 551.59, low-quality evidence) but did not significantly increase for adequately nourished women. Protein intake increased significantly (MD +6.99 g/day, 95% CI 3.02 to 10.97). No significant differences were observed for neonatal death, stillbirth, small-for-gestational-age infants, or total gestational weight gain. Data on perinatal death were not available. Balanced Energy and Protein Supplementation Balanced energy and protein supplementation significantly reduced the risk of stillbirth (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.94, moderate-quality evidence). Mean birthweight increased significantly (MD +40.96 g, 95% CI 4.66 to 77.26, moderate-quality evidence). The risk of small-for-gestational-age infants was reduced (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.90, moderate-quality evidence). No significant effects were observed for preterm birth, neonatal death, or weekly gestational weight gain. Data on perinatal death and low birthweight were not reported. High-Protein Supplementation High-protein supplementation was associated with an increased risk of small-for-gestational-age infants (RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.03 to 2.41, moderate-quality evidence). No significant effects were observed for stillbirth, neonatal death, preterm birth, birthweight, or weekly gestational weight gain. Data on perinatal death were not reported. Isocaloric Protein Supplementation Isocaloric protein supplementation had no significant effects on birthweight or weekly gestational weight gain. Data on perinatal mortality, stillbirth, neonatal death, small-for-gestational-age infants, and preterm birth were not reported. Conclusions Nutritional education aimed at increasing energy and protein intake appears to reduce the risk of preterm birth and low birthweight, increase head circumference at birth, and improve birthweight among undernourished women. However, it does not appear to affect other outcomes significantly. Balanced energy and protein supplementation improves fetal growth and reduces the risk of stillbirth and small-for-gestational-age infants. High-protein supplementation may be harmful, as it increases the risk of small-for-gestational-age infants. Isocaloric protein supplementation alone does not appear to have significant effects on perinatal outcomes. The findings should be interpreted with caution due to unclear or high risk of bias in several trials and the low quality of evidence for many outcomes. Future interventions should target women who are most likely to benefit, particularly those with energy and protein intake below recommended levels. Large, well-designed randomized trials are needed to further assess the effects of increasing energy and protein intake during pregnancy.
